text: You're given a list of intervals. They're sorted by start, and no two of them overlap. Insert one new interval, merge anything that overlaps, and return the result, still sorted and non-overlapping.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if two intervals only touch, like one to three and three to five, do they count as overlapping? And can the input list be empty?
Touching counts as overlapping, so those two become one to five. And yes, the list can be empty.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: since the list is sorted and nothing overlaps, the ends are sorted too. So the intervals that overlap the new one have to sit together in one block in the middle. Everything before that block is fully to the left, everything after is fully to the right. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth intervals, and every value is between zero and ten to the fifth.

Got it. No sums anywhere, so a regular int is fine. Let me check the examples. One to three and six to nine, insert two to five. Two to five touches one to three, so they merge into one to five, and six to nine stays. Second example, insert four to eight. It swallows three to five, six to seven, and eight to ten — eight touches eight — so I get one to two, three to ten, twelve to sixteen. Both match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would append the new interval, sort everything, and merge. That's n log n, and it throws away the fact that the input is already sorted. Binary search could find the overlapping block faster, but I still have to copy every interval into the output, so it stays linear. This problem reminds me of a linear sweep over sorted intervals. One pointer, three phases: copy the ones on the left, absorb the ones that overlap, copy the ones on the right.
How do you know the three phases cover every case?

Because of the block I mentioned. An interval is either fully left, overlapping, or fully right, and they come in that order. I also checked it. Against the sort-and-merge version, I ran every sorted, non-overlapping list on coordinates zero to seven with every new interval — about fifty-seven thousand cases — plus twenty thousand random ones. Zero mismatches.

Here's the plan, in three steps. First, while the current interval ends before the new one starts, copy it. Second, while the new one's end reaches the current start, absorb it: take the smaller start and the larger end. When that stops, push the new interval. Third, copy everything that's left. One thing worth flagging — the comparisons. The first loop is strictly less than, the second is greater than or equal. Touching has to count as overlap.

Alright. Three while loops sharing one index. The first copies intervals whose end is smaller than the new start. The second absorbs: new start becomes the min, new end becomes the max. Then I push the new interval — outside the loop, so it's added even if nothing overlapped. The third copies the rest. The easy line to get wrong is the first loop's condition. If I write less than or equal, one to three plus three to five comes back as two pieces. And here's the scary part: both official examples still pass with that bug. Out of about fifty-seven thousand small cases, it fails twenty-five thousand.

Let's dry-run example two, expected one to two, three to ten, twelve to sixteen. The row that matters is index three, eight to ten. The new interval is three to eight at that point, and eight is greater than or equal to eight, so it's absorbed and the end grows to ten. With a strict comparison it would stop at three to eight and split the answer. Corner cases: an empty list gives just the new interval. New inside an existing one gives that one back. New before everything goes first. New after everything goes last.

Let me think about complexity here. The index only moves forward, so all three loops together take n steps. Time is linear. Space is linear too, but that's all output; besides the result I only keep the index and the size. In the worst case for output, the new interval goes after ten thousand intervals and I return ten thousand and one.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You noticed the overlapping intervals form one contiguous block, which is why one pass works. You were careful about touching intervals, and you knew the official examples wouldn't catch that mistake. And you explained why binary search doesn't beat linear time here. Good work.
